title: Window deltas of critical error counters
claim: Adding per-disk deltas over the 14-day window (last - first, last - value 3 days before cutoff, last - value 7 days before) for smart_5/187/188/197/198/199 raw will raise AUPRC and R@FAR over cutoff-day snapshots.
rationale: Backblaze notes these counters (except 197) are cumulative, so a jump from 0 to 20 in a day signals far more risk than 60 errors accrued over years; Botezatu and Zhu both use change-over-time representations.
applicability: All vendors; 187/188 mostly Seagate (NaN elsewhere). Requires sorting history by date per serial.
expected_effect: Large: typically the single biggest gain over init.py's snapshot features (AUPRC +several points).
risk: Disks with fewer than 4 rows give noisy deltas; counter resets (negative deltas) must be clipped or flagged.
impl_hint: g=h.sort_values('date').groupby('serial_number'); for c in COLS: f[c+'_d14']=g[c].last()-g[c].first(); use shift-by-date via pivot (serial x day_index) for d3/d7; clip at 0 and add a 'counter_reset' flag.
idea: Adding per-disk deltas over the 14-day window (last - first, last - value 3 days before cutoff, last - value 7 days before) for smart_5/187/188/197/198/199 raw will raise AUPRC and R@FAR over cutoff-day snapshots.

title: Error growth rate normalised by observed days
claim: Dividing each counter delta by the number of observed days (not calendar days) and using log1p(rate) for smart_5/187/197/198 will make trend features comparable across disks with missing days and short histories.
rationale: Missing days and new disks (<14 rows) are explicitly present in this benchmark; rate-based features are robust to them and mirror Backblaze's 'errors per time' reasoning.
applicability: Any disk with >=2 rows; set NaN when only one row.
expected_effect: Medium; mostly improves robustness (F1_p10) rather than peak AUPRC.
risk: Division by very small spans can explode; cap spans at >=1 day.
impl_hint: rate = (last-first)/max(1,(date_last-date_first).days); feature=np.log1p(rate.clip(0)).
idea: Dividing each counter delta by the number of observed days (not calendar days) and using log1p(rate) for smart_5/187/197/198 will make trend features comparable across disks with missing days and short histories.

title: First-appearance flags for reallocation/pending/uncorrectable
claim: Binary features 'became non-zero inside the window' and 'days since the counter first became non-zero' for smart_5, 197, 198 and 187 will sharpen the very top of the ranking (R@FAR).
rationale: Google found the first scan error raises 60-day failure risk 39x and first reallocation 14x; a counter that just turned on is a fresher signal than a long-standing non-zero value.
applicability: All vendors; days-since is capped at window length (14) when already non-zero at window start.
expected_effect: Medium-large at the top of the ranking; cheap to compute.
risk: Long-standing non-zero drives (stable old reallocations) are common among healthy disks; do not treat any non-zero as alarm.
impl_hint: nz=(pivot>0); became=(~nz.iloc[:,0]) & nz.iloc[:,-1]; days_since_first = n_days - argmax(nz, axis=1) (NaN if never).
idea: Binary features 'became non-zero inside the window' and 'days since the counter first became non-zero' for smart_5, 197, 198 and 187 will sharpen the very top of the ranking (R@FAR).

title: Count of critical SMART attributes firing and increasing
claim: Features n_crit_nonzero = count of {5,187,188,197,198} raw > 0 at cutoff and n_crit_increasing = count with positive 14-day delta will be among the top-5 LightGBM gain features.
rationale: Backblaze: 76.7% of failed vs 4.2% of operational drives have at least one of these >0, and the attributes are mostly independent (except 197/198), so their count aggregates independent evidence.
applicability: All vendors; count only attributes that are reported (non-NaN) and also add n_crit_reported.
expected_effect: Medium; helps linear models greatly and trees modestly.
risk: Vendors without 187/188 have lower max counts; include n_crit_reported to avoid vendor confounding.
impl_hint: crit=['smart_5_raw','smart_187_raw','smart_188_raw','smart_197_raw','smart_198_raw']; last[crit].gt(0).sum(1); (delta[crit]>0).sum(1); last[crit].notna().sum(1).
idea: Features n_crit_nonzero = count of {5,187,188,197,198} raw > 0 at cutoff and n_crit_increasing = count with positive 14-day delta will be among the top-5 LightGBM gain features.

title: Treat smart_197 (pending) as a state, not a counter
claim: Using max, last and (last - max) of smart_197_raw over the window, plus the joint pattern '197 falling while smart_5 rising' (pending sectors being reallocated), will add signal beyond delta features.
rationale: Backblaze states 197 is the only non-cumulative attribute among its five; pending sectors can be resolved or remapped, so its trajectory (peak and conversion into reallocations) matters.
applicability: All vendors reporting 197 (nearly all).
risk: Pattern features are sparse; keep them numeric (not rules) so the model can ignore them.
impl_hint: f['s197_max']=g.max(); f['s197_drop']=f['s197_max']-last197; f['realloc_from_pending']=(f['s197_drop']>0)&(d5>0).
idea: Using max, last and (last - max) of smart_197_raw over the window, plus the joint pattern '197 falling while smart_5 rising' (pending sectors being reallocated), will add signal beyond delta features.

title: Multi-scale window statistics (3/7/14 days)
claim: Computing max, mean, std and least-squares slope over the last 3, 7 and 14 days for the critical counters and for smart_1/7 normalized will outperform a single 14-day aggregate.
rationale: Positives' cutoffs are 1-7 days before failure, so symptoms often appear in the last few days; Botezatu's compact time-series representation and PAKDD winners' sliding-window features both use several scales.
applicability: Requires day-indexed pivot; windows shorter than available history degrade gracefully to NaN.
expected_effect: Medium; larger for AUPRC than for F1.
risk: Feature count grows fast (attrs x stats x windows); restrict to ~10 attributes to stay far under the 600 s budget.
impl_hint: Build a (serial, day_offset 0..13) array via pivot_table; slope = cov(t,x)/var(t) vectorised in numpy; avoid per-serial Python loops.
idea: Computing max, mean, std and least-squares slope over the last 3, 7 and 14 days for the critical counters and for smart_1/7 normalized will outperform a single 14-day aggregate.

title: Drops in vendor-normalized health values
claim: Features 'min over window' and 'first - last' of smart_1/3/5/7/187/197/198 _normalized will help on vendors where raw values are encoded or unavailable.
rationale: Normalized values are vendor-scaled health scores (lower = worse); Backblaze publishes both raw and normalized, and many prior studies (StreamDFP, Botezatu) use both representations.
applicability: All vendors; especially useful for smart_1 and smart_7 on Seagate where raw values are not simple counts.
risk: Normalized scales differ by vendor/model; combine with vendor/model feature (FE09).
impl_hint: for a in [1,3,5,7,187,197,198]: f[f'n{a}_min']=g[f'smart_{a}_normalized'].min(); f[f'n{a}_drop']=first-last.
idea: Features 'min over window' and 'first - last' of smart_1/3/5/7/187/197/198 _normalized will help on vendors where raw values are encoded or unavailable.

title: Per-model rank normalization of vendor-specific raw attributes
claim: Replacing raw smart_1/7/9/193/240/241/242 values with their percentile rank within the same model (computed on train+query features, no labels) will reduce vendor confounding and improve transfer across the 44 models.
rationale: Attribute semantics and scales differ by vendor/model (heterogeneous reliability and reporting); per-model normalisation acts as simple domain alignment, akin to the source/target alignment in transfer work.
applicability: Models with at least ~30 disks; fall back to vendor-level rank for tiny models.
expected_effect: Medium for minority models; neutral on Seagate-dominated majority.
risk: Using query-set features is transductive (allowed: no labels, no post-cutoff data) but ranks shift between splits; prefer train-only stats if val/test fleets differ strongly.
impl_hint: last['model_rank_'+c]=last.groupby('model')[c].rank(pct=True); for models with <30 disks use groupby(vendor).
idea: Replacing raw smart_1/7/9/193/240/241/242 values with their percentile rank within the same model (computed on train+query features, no labels) will reduce vendor confounding and improve transfer across the 44 models.

title: Model identity and model-level failure prior
claim: Adding 'model' as a LightGBM categorical feature plus an out-of-fold smoothed target encoding of model failure rate will raise AUPRC because per-model AFR varies by >10x.
rationale: Backblaze 2024 per-model AFR ranges 0.22%-11.38%; manufacturer differences persist after controlling for age and capacity; heterogeneity is a first-order effect.
applicability: All disks; unseen models in query fall back to vendor prior.
risk: Target encoding must be computed out-of-fold (grouped by serial) or it leaks; per-model rates in Q3 may shift in Q4.
impl_hint: te = (pos_in_model + a*global_rate)/(n_in_model + a) with a~50, computed within CV folds; model -> pd.Categorical for LightGBM categorical_feature.
idea: Adding 'model' as a LightGBM categorical feature plus an out-of-fold smoothed target encoding of model failure rate will raise AUPRC because per-model AFR varies by >10x.

title: Age and head-flying-hours with interactions
claim: Using smart_9_raw/24 (age in days), smart_240_raw and capacity_bytes as features, letting the tree model form age x error interactions, will modestly improve ranking.
rationale: Failure rates depend on life stage (early wear-out, late spike), and splitting populations by age or head-flying hours improved RF accuracy; smart_9 is Backblaze's own age proxy.
applicability: All vendors (smart_240 missing on some).
expected_effect: Small-medium; mainly helps distinguish old disks with stable reallocations from young disks with new errors.
risk: Age alone is weakly predictive and shifts over quarters as the fleet ages; do not rely on absolute thresholds.
impl_hint: f['age_days']=last.smart_9_raw/24; f['hfh_ratio']=last.smart_240_raw/last.smart_9_raw.
idea: Using smart_9_raw/24 (age in days), smart_240_raw and capacity_bytes as features, letting the tree model form age x error interactions, will modestly improve ranking.

title: Missing-day and history-length features
claim: Features n_rows_in_window, max_gap_days, gap_before_cutoff and is_new_disk (<14 rows) will add signal because failing disks tend to have irregular telemetry before failure.
rationale: The benchmark documents missing days and short histories; production studies (RODMAN) show missing samples are common and non-random around failures.
applicability: All disks.
risk: Could encode sampling artefacts of the benchmark rather than physics; check OOF importance and val stability.
impl_hint: d=h.groupby('serial_number')['date']; f['n_rows']=d.size(); f['max_gap']=d.apply(lambda s: s.diff().dt.days.max()) -> vectorise via sorted diff + groupby max.
idea: Features n_rows_in_window, max_gap_days, gap_before_cutoff and is_new_disk (<14 rows) will add signal because failing disks tend to have irregular telemetry before failure.

title: Keep NaN for unreported attributes instead of fillna(0)
claim: Leaving unreported SMART attributes as NaN (LightGBM's native missing handling) plus is_reported flags will beat fillna(0), which conflates 'not reported' with 'zero errors'.
rationale: Attribute sets differ by vendor (187/188/190 mostly Seagate); zero-filling makes non-Seagate disks look perfectly healthy on those axes and injects vendor confounding.
applicability: Tree models; for logistic regression impute with per-vendor median plus missing flags.
risk: None significant for GBDT.
impl_hint: Do not call fillna before LightGBM; for sklearn models use SimpleImputer(add_indicator=True).
idea: Leaving unreported SMART attributes as NaN (LightGBM's native missing handling) plus is_reported flags will beat fillna(0), which conflates 'not reported' with 'zero errors'.

title: Workload proxies from LBAs written/read and power events
claim: 14-day deltas of smart_241/242 (LBAs written/read), smart_12 (power cycles), smart_192 (power-off retracts) and smart_4 (start/stop) will add a small independent signal.
rationale: Lu et al. show performance/workload features add predictive power beyond SMART error counters; Backblaze saw failed drives power-cycled ~2.7x more; Pinciroli links head-positioning time to failures.
applicability: Vendors reporting 241/242 (Seagate, some others).
risk: Workload differs by data-center role, not disk health; may overfit Q3-specific operations.
impl_hint: Same delta machinery as FE01; log1p the LBA deltas.
idea: 14-day deltas of smart_241/242 (LBAs written/read), smart_12 (power cycles), smart_192 (power-off retracts) and smart_4 (start/stop) will add a small independent signal.

title: Temperature is a weak, low-priority feature
claim: Including smart_194 mean/max/std over the window will add at most marginal gain; spend evolution budget elsewhere first.
rationale: Google found temperature and activity much less correlated with failure than previously believed; manufacturer-difference study controls for temperature with modest effect.
applicability: All vendors.
risk: Temperature correlates with rack location/season; may encode drift.
impl_hint: Keep only smart_194 max and std if already computed; don't build many temperature variants.
idea: Including smart_194 mean/max/std over the window will add at most marginal gain; spend evolution budget elsewhere first.

title: Statistical feature selection per attribute (rank-sum / changepoint)
claim: Screening candidate features with a Wilcoxon rank-sum test (failed vs healthy, per vendor) and dropping those with no signal will reduce noise and runtime without hurting AUPRC.
rationale: Hughes et al. use rank-sum tests for failure warnings; Botezatu uses changepoint detection to pick informative SMART parameters; WEFR shows ensemble feature ranking generalises across models.
applicability: When the feature set exceeds ~150 columns or runtime approaches budget.
expected_effect: Small accuracy gain, useful runtime reduction.
risk: Selection must be done inside CV folds or it biases OOF estimates.
impl_hint: scipy.stats.mannwhitneyu per feature on training fold; keep features with p<1e-3 or top-k by LightGBM gain averaged over folds.
idea: Screening candidate features with a Wilcoxon rank-sum test (failed vs healthy, per vendor) and dropping those with no signal will reduce noise and runtime without hurting AUPRC.

title: LightGBM on engineered window features
claim: Replacing logistic regression with LightGBM (num_leaves 15-31, learning_rate 0.03-0.05, 300-800 rounds, min_child_samples 20-50, feature_fraction 0.7, bagging_fraction 0.8) on FE01-FE12 features will be the largest single jump in ROS.
rationale: Tree ensembles (CART, RF, RGF, GBDT/FastTree, LightGBM) dominate SMART failure prediction in production and competitions; LightGBM is fast and handles NaN natively.
applicability: Always; ~31k training disks x ~150 features trains in seconds.
expected_effect: Large (commonly +10-20 ROS points over the LR baseline when combined with FE01).
risk: Overfitting to 1104 positives; keep leaves small and use early stopping on OOF folds.
impl_hint: lgb.LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=600, learning_rate=0.03, num_leaves=31, min_child_samples=30, subsample=0.8, subsample_freq=1, colsample_bytree=0.7, reg_lambda=1.0, n_jobs=-1, verbose=-1).
idea: Replacing logistic regression with LightGBM (num_leaves 15-31, learning_rate 0.03-0.05, 300-800 rounds, min_child_samples 20-50, feature_fraction 0.7, bagging_fraction 0.8) on FE01-FE12 features will be the largest single jump in ROS.

title: Random forest / ExtraTrees as a robust second learner
claim: An ExtraTreesClassifier or RandomForest (300-500 trees, min_samples_leaf 3-10, class_weight='balanced_subsample') trained on the same features and rank-averaged with LightGBM will improve F1_p10 via variance reduction.
rationale: Random forests are repeatedly the strongest or near-strongest model for HDD/SSD failure prediction (Mahdisoltani, Pinciroli, Alter, Xiao's online RF); different inductive bias from boosting.
applicability: When LightGBM alone plateaus; sklearn needs NaN imputed (use -1 sentinel).
risk: Runtime with many trees; set n_jobs=-1 and max_features='sqrt'.
impl_hint: ExtraTreesClassifier(n_estimators=400, min_samples_leaf=5, max_features='sqrt', class_weight='balanced_subsample', n_jobs=-1).fit(X.fillna(-1), y).
idea: An ExtraTreesClassifier or RandomForest (300-500 trees, min_samples_leaf 3-10, class_weight='balanced_subsample') trained on the same features and rank-averaged with LightGBM will improve F1_p10 via variance reduction.
source: mahdisoltani2017, pinciroli2022, alter2019, xiao2018, botezatu2016, amram2021

title: Ranking objective for the top of the list
claim: Training LightGBM with objective='lambdarank' (single query group, or groups by vendor) or with a heavy positive weight will improve R@FAR and AUPRC because the metric only rewards the top ~0.2%-2% of disks.
rationale: Microsoft's CDEF uses a cost-sensitive ranking model over disks and selects the top-r; the benchmark's R@FAR and AUPRC are ranking metrics dominated by the head of the list.
applicability: After a binary LightGBM baseline exists; compare OOF weighted AUPRC.
risk: lambdarank with 31k items in one group is slow/unstable; groups by cutoff week are a practical alternative.
impl_hint: LGBMRanker(objective='lambdarank', label_gain=[0,1]) with group sizes from cutoff_date week; convert score to rank for output.
idea: Training LightGBM with objective='lambdarank' (single query group, or groups by vendor) or with a heavy positive weight will improve R@FAR and AUPRC because the metric only rewards the top ~0.2%-2% of disks.

title: Global model with vendor features beats per-vendor models
claim: A single pooled model with vendor/model features will outperform separate per-vendor models for Toshiba/HGST/WDC, which have few failures; keep per-vendor models only as ensemble members.
rationale: Transfer-learning work shows minority disk models benefit from borrowing strength from failure-rich models; Botezatu uses transfer for new models with scarce labels.
applicability: Always test: per-vendor split only if the vendor has >=200 positives in train.
risk: A pooled model may under-fit Seagate-specific attributes (187/188); mitigate via interactions (trees) or by adding a Seagate-only member.
impl_hint: Train one LGBM with 'vendor' and 'model' categoricals; optionally a Seagate-only LGBM whose score replaces the global score for ST* disks when OOF AUPRC is higher.
idea: A single pooled model with vendor/model features will outperform separate per-vendor models for Toshiba/HGST/WDC, which have few failures; keep per-vendor models only as ensemble members.

title: Skip deep sequence models under the 600 s budget
claim: Do not spend iterations on LSTM/CNN-LSTM/Transformer models; hand-crafted window features with GBDT will match them on 14-day windows at a fraction of the runtime.
rationale: Deep models (RNN, CNN-LSTM, TFBEST) shine with long sequences and extra signals; here windows are <=14 days, only pandas/numpy/sklearn/lightgbm/scipy are allowed, and runtime beyond 600 s is penalised.
applicability: This benchmark's dependency and runtime constraints.
risk: May leave small gains from sequence modelling on the table.
impl_hint: If a sequence signal is wanted, use sklearn MLPClassifier on the flattened 14-day pivot as a cheap ensemble member.
idea: Do not spend iterations on LSTM/CNN-LSTM/Transformer models; hand-crafted window features with GBDT will match them on 14-day windows at a fraction of the runtime.

title: Unsupervised anomaly score as an extra feature
claim: An IsolationForest (or per-vendor robust z-score sum) fit on healthy training disks' window features, fed as a feature or blended with low weight, may recover some failures with no classic SMART error signal.
rationale: 23-36% of failed drives show no SMART error counters; rank-sum/anomaly tests against healthy references (Hughes) capture subtler deviations.
applicability: After the supervised pipeline is stable.
risk: Anomaly scores also flag harmless outliers (new models, odd firmware) and can increase false alarms.
impl_hint: IsolationForest(n_estimators=200, contamination='auto').fit(X_healthy.fillna(-1)); add -score_samples as feature inside CV.
idea: An IsolationForest (or per-vendor robust z-score sum) fit on healthy training disks' window features, fed as a feature or blended with low weight, may recover some failures with no classic SMART error signal.

title: Tune positive weighting against the fleet weights
claim: Training with sample_weight = fleet weight for negatives (about 10) and positive weight scaled so the positive class carries 10-30% of total weight will give better weighted AUPRC than either raw fleet weights or unweighted training.
rationale: Cost-sensitive learning is the most common algorithm-level fix for Backblaze imbalance; the metric uses fleet weights, so training weights control where the model spends capacity.
applicability: Any weighted learner; select the ratio via OOF weighted AUPRC.
risk: Extreme positive weights inflate scores for noisy positives and raise false alarms; retune the threshold whenever weights change.
impl_hint: w = np.where(y==1, pos_w, fleet_w); try pos_w in {1, 5, 10, 30}; pick by OOF weighted AUPRC.
idea: Training with sample_weight = fleet weight for negatives (about 10) and positive weight scaled so the positive class carries 10-30% of total weight will give better weighted AUPRC than either raw fleet weights or unweighted training.

title: Negative-subsampling bagging ensemble
claim: Training K=5-10 LightGBM models, each on all positives plus a different random 30-50% of negatives, and averaging their ranks will improve F1_p10 stability.
rationale: Informed/Poisson downsampling of healthy disks with bagging is used by Botezatu, Xiao (online bagging) and StreamDFP (lambda_p > lambda_n); it reduces variance and speeds training.
applicability: When single-model scores fluctuate across seeds or folds.
risk: Runtime multiplies by K; keep each model small.
impl_hint: for k in range(K): idx = pos_idx U rng.choice(neg_idx, int(0.4*len(neg_idx))); fit; preds.append(rankdata(model.predict_proba(Xq)[:,1]))
idea: Training K=5-10 LightGBM models, each on all positives plus a different random 30-50% of negatives, and averaging their ranks will improve F1_p10 stability.

title: Prefer cost-sensitive weighting over SMOTE
claim: Using class weights instead of SMOTE/CTGAN oversampling will give equal or better OOF AUPRC with less risk for GBDT on heavy-tailed SMART counters.
rationale: SMOTE interpolates between neighbours, which is ill-suited to integer, heavy-tailed, vendor-dependent counters; oversampling before splitting is a known leakage source.
applicability: GBDT/RF pipelines.
risk: Very small minority vendors might still benefit from oversampling; only apply inside training folds.
impl_hint: If trying SMOTE at all, implement it manually with numpy inside the CV loop (imblearn is not an allowed dependency).
idea: Using class weights instead of SMOTE/CTGAN oversampling will give equal or better OOF AUPRC with less risk for GBDT on heavy-tailed SMART counters.

title: Exploit the 1-7 day horizon: recent-day features first
claim: Features measured on the last 1-3 days before cutoff (e.g., smart_5/197/198 delta over the last 2 days) will carry more signal than 14-day aggregates because every positive fails 1-7 days after cutoff.
rationale: prepare_data.py sets positive cutoff = failure day - k with k uniform in 1..7; prediction quality drops with longer lead times (Lu), and short horizons are easiest (Alter).
applicability: This benchmark's sampling design.
risk: Last-day-only features are noisy for disks with gaps near cutoff; pair with FE11 gap features.
impl_hint: d2 = value at cutoff - value at cutoff-2 days (by date, not row index).
idea: Features measured on the last 1-3 days before cutoff (e.g., smart_5/197/198 delta over the last 2 days) will carry more signal than 14-day aggregates because every positive fails 1-7 days after cutoff.

title: Window-shift augmentation of training samples
claim: Creating extra training samples from each training disk's history truncated to end at cutoff-1..cutoff-3 (negatives stay negative; positives labeled positive with lower weight 0.3-0.6) will enlarge the positive set and improve recall.
rationale: A negative alive at c+7 is also alive 7 days after any earlier day, so shifted negatives are exact; shifted positives fail within 8-10 days, a softer positive. This mirrors StreamDFP's extra labeled pre-failure days, RODMAN's pre-failure backtracking and multiple-instance framing.
applicability: Training data only; features must be computed identically on truncated histories.
expected_effect: Medium, uncertain; biggest on recall at fixed FAR.
risk: Shifted positives are further from failure than the query distribution; too much weight blurs the decision boundary and increases false alarms. Correlated duplicates: keep all shifts of one disk in the same CV fold.
impl_hint: for s in [1,2,3]: hist_s = hist[hist.date <= cutoff - s days]; X_s = featurize(hist_s); w_s = fleet_w (neg) or 0.5 (pos); concatenate with group id = serial.
idea: Creating extra training samples from each training disk's history truncated to end at cutoff-1..cutoff-3 (negatives stay negative; positives labeled positive with lower weight 0.3-0.6) will enlarge the positive set and improve recall.

title: Do not overfit silent failures
claim: Regularising the model (min_child_samples >= 30, max_depth <= 6) and optionally down-weighting positives with no SMART change at all (all critical counters flat and zero) to 0.3 will improve precision and F1_p10 without real recall loss.
rationale: 23.3% (Backblaze) to ~36% (Google) of failed drives show no SMART error signal; forcing the model to separate them from healthy disks mainly fits noise. Failure-type filtering in RODMAN is the production analogue.
applicability: Training weights only; never drop query disks.
risk: Some 'silent' positives are predictable via workload/normalized features; verify via OOF that recall at FAR 0.2% does not drop.
impl_hint: silent = (y==1) & (last[crit].fillna(0).sum(1)==0) & (delta[crit].fillna(0).sum(1)==0); w[silent]*=0.3.
idea: Regularising the model (min_child_samples >= 30, max_depth <= 6) and optionally down-weighting positives with no SMART change at all (all critical counters flat and zero) to 0.3 will improve precision and F1_p10 without real recall loss.

title: Backblaze failure semantics
claim: Assume label=1 means Backblaze marked the drive failed (it stops being logged), while drives removed for upgrades are not failures; therefore do not use 'disk disappears' logic and do not treat end-of-history as a signal.
rationale: Backblaze documents that failed drives are marked and removed; decommissioned healthy drives are not failures. The benchmark's per-disk cutoff design prevents disappearance leakage by construction.
applicability: Always.
expected_effect: Avoids a class of invalid ideas.
risk: None.
impl_hint: No code; guidance for the LLM when proposing features.
idea: Assume label=1 means Backblaze marked the drive failed (it stops being logged), while drives removed for upgrades are not failures; therefore do not use 'disk disappears' logic and do not treat end-of-history as a signal.

title: Replicate ROS on out-of-fold predictions
claim: Implementing the evaluator's weighted F1_p10 (200 stratified bootstraps), weighted AUPRC and R@FAR(0.2%) on grouped 5-fold OOF training predictions, and using it for model/threshold selection, will correlate far better with val ROS than training-set F1.
rationale: The score combines three metrics with specific weighting and bootstrapping; selecting on a proxy (accuracy, ROC-AUC, in-sample F1) misaligns the search.
applicability: Always; costs a few seconds.
expected_effect: Medium indirect gain (better selection of thresholds and hyper-parameters).
risk: Q3 OOF still differs from Q4 val (drift); treat OOF as ranking signal, not absolute truth.
impl_hint: Copy weighted_auprc / recall_at_far / bootstrap_f1 logic (numpy only) into the solution; StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0) on disks (one row per disk already).
idea: Implementing the evaluator's weighted F1_p10 (200 stratified bootstraps), weighted AUPRC and R@FAR(0.2%) on grouped 5-fold OOF training predictions, and using it for model/threshold selection, will correlate far better with val ROS than training-set F1.

title: Understand the FAR budget in sample counts
claim: Aiming for the top ~60 sampled healthy disks (0.2% of weighted negatives) to contain almost no negatives will maximise R@FAR, so boost disks with rapid multi-attribute error growth to the very top of the score.
rationale: Each sampled negative represents ~10 fleet disks, so FAR 0.2% of ~300k weighted negatives allows only ~60 sampled false positives; only near-certain signals (large 5/197/198/187 jumps) belong there. FDR-at-low-FAR operating points are standard in the literature.
applicability: Scoring/ranking design.
expected_effect: Guides the score design for 20% of ROS.
risk: Over-boosting rules can hurt AUPRC in the middle of the ranking.
impl_hint: Check OOF: sort by score, count negatives among the top-N until cum negative weight / total negative weight > 0.002.
idea: Aiming for the top ~60 sampled healthy disks (0.2% of weighted negatives) to contain almost no negatives will maximise R@FAR, so boost disks with rapid multi-attribute error growth to the very top of the score.

title: Weighted precision punishes every false alarm ~10x
claim: Alarm sets should be small and precise: with fleet weights, each false alarm costs ~10 weighted FP, so the F1-optimal alarm count is usually at or below the number of true positives the model can catch at >50% precision.
rationale: Weighted F1 uses fleet weights (negatives ~10); init.py's quantile-scan threshold ignores this. Accuracy is not enough; operational metrics must reflect the cost of wasted replacements (Li 2016).
applicability: Threshold selection.
expected_effect: Medium impact on the 50% F1_p10 term.
risk: Too few alarms makes bootstrap F1 high-variance and lowers the 10th percentile.
impl_hint: Scan thresholds on OOF scores with weighted counts: tp=sum(w*y*a), fp=sum(w*(1-y)*a).
idea: Alarm sets should be small and precise: with fleet weights, each false alarm costs ~10 weighted FP, so the F1-optimal alarm count is usually at or below the number of true positives the model can catch at >50% precision.

title: Validate by disk group and time, never by row
claim: Keeping all rows (and augmented shifts) of one serial in the same CV fold and never fitting encoders/scalers on validation folds will avoid optimistic OOF estimates that don't transfer to Q4/Q1.
rationale: Row-level random splits leak on Backblaze and inflate metrics (Grillmeyer 2025); temporal adjacency matters under drift (Lyu 2025).
applicability: Any CV, target encoding, feature selection, or stacking.
expected_effect: Prevents selection errors; no direct score gain.
risk: None.
impl_hint: GroupKFold/StratifiedGroupKFold (sklearn >=1.0) with groups=serial_number; also compute OOF by cutoff-date blocks to sanity-check drift.
idea: Keeping all rows (and augmented shifts) of one serial in the same CV fold and never fitting encoders/scalers on validation folds will avoid optimistic OOF estimates that don't transfer to Q4/Q1.

title: Stay under the 600 s time budget
claim: Keeping total runtime (I/O + features + training + prediction) under ~300 s with vectorised pandas/numpy and n_jobs=-1 will avoid the time_factor penalty (min(1, 600/runtime)) and the 900 s hard fail.
rationale: time_factor multiplies the whole score; a 1200 s run halves ROS. The history files are ~31k disks x <=14 rows per split, so vectorised code is seconds; Python per-disk loops are the usual culprit.
applicability: Always.
risk: Bagging/ensembles and nested CV multiply runtime; measure with time.time() and cap K.
impl_hint: Read CSVs with usecols and dtype float32; use groupby().agg over a list of columns; avoid groupby.apply with lambdas.
idea: Keeping total runtime (I/O + features + training + prediction) under ~300 s with vectorised pandas/numpy and n_jobs=-1 will avoid the time_factor penalty (min(1, 600/runtime)) and the 900 s hard fail.

title: Prefer PR-based selection over ROC-AUC
claim: Selecting models and hyper-parameters by weighted AUPRC (and R@FAR), not ROC-AUC, will pick models with better early retrieval, which is what 50% of ROS actually measures.
rationale: Under ~0.25% fleet prevalence, ROC-AUC is insensitive to top-of-list quality while PR curves expose it.
applicability: Model selection.
risk: PR metrics are noisier with ~1100 positives; average across folds/seeds.
impl_hint: Use the evaluator's weighted_auprc on OOF, averaged over 5 folds x 2 seeds.
idea: Selecting models and hyper-parameters by weighted AUPRC (and R@FAR), not ROC-AUC, will pick models with better early retrieval, which is what 50% of ROS actually measures.

title: Pick the alarm threshold on OOF scores, not in-sample
claim: Choosing the alarm threshold from grouped 5-fold OOF probabilities (instead of in-sample training predictions like init.py) will raise val F1 and F1_p10, because in-sample scores of boosted trees are overconfident.
rationale: Threshold optimality depends on both classes' score distributions (Lipton); in-sample scores of flexible models are shifted upward for positives, making the chosen threshold too low/high on new data.
applicability: Any model with alarm output.
risk: OOF threshold then applied to a model refit on all data: refit changes score scale slightly; either average fold models for query prediction or use rank-based thresholds.
impl_hint: Predict the query set with the average of the 5 fold models so query scores share the OOF score scale; threshold = argmax over OOF grid.
idea: Choosing the alarm threshold from grouped 5-fold OOF probabilities (instead of in-sample training predictions like init.py) will raise val F1 and F1_p10, because in-sample scores of boosted trees are overconfident.

title: Maximise the bootstrap 10th percentile, choose on a plateau
claim: Selecting the threshold that maximises the 10th percentile of bootstrap weighted F1 on OOF predictions (or the centre of the region within 97% of max F1) will beat argmax point F1 on val F1_p10.
rationale: The evaluator rewards robust thresholds via F1_p10 over 200 stratified bootstraps; a lucky spike in the F1 curve does not survive resampling or the Q3->Q4 shift.
applicability: After T01.
risk: Bootstrapping inside the solution costs time; 100 resamples over a 50-point grid is <1 s with vectorised numpy.
impl_hint: grid = np.quantile(oof, np.linspace(0.95, 0.999, 80)); for t in grid compute p10 of bootstrap F1; pick argmax (tie-break toward lower threshold).
idea: Selecting the threshold that maximises the 10th percentile of bootstrap weighted F1 on OOF predictions (or the centre of the region within 97% of max F1) will beat argmax point F1 on val F1_p10.

title: Probability thresholds transfer better than alarm-rate thresholds
claim: Using a fixed probability threshold (from OOF, possibly near maxF1/2 for calibrated scores) rather than a fixed top-x% quantile will be more robust to the prevalence change between train (1104 positives), val (756) and test (770).
rationale: The number of failures per quarter changes, so a fixed alarm fraction would over- or under-alarm; Lipton et al. show calibrated F1-optimal thresholds are about half the achievable F1, independent of the query set's size.
applicability: When scores are reasonably calibrated (LightGBM binary objective without extreme weights, or after Platt/isotonic on OOF).
risk: Calibration differs across vendors; a single probability threshold may over-alarm Seagate and under-alarm others.
impl_hint: iso = IsotonicRegression(out_of_bounds='clip').fit(oof, y, sample_weight=w); alarm = iso.predict(q) >= t_prob.
idea: Using a fixed probability threshold (from OOF, possibly near maxF1/2 for calibrated scores) rather than a fixed top-x% quantile will be more robust to the prevalence change between train (1104 positives), val (756) and test (770).

title: Rule guardrails layered on the ML score
claim: Forcing alarm=1 and a score boost for disks whose smart_5, 197 or 198 increased by a large amount inside the window (e.g., top-0.1% delta in train) while keeping ML alarms elsewhere will lift R@FAR and F1 slightly.
rationale: RAIDShield's reallocation-threshold policy and Backblaze's replace-on-187>0 practice show extreme counter growth is near-deterministic; but the pure rule baseline scores only ROS ~12.9, so rules must be a guardrail, not the model.
applicability: Use thresholds learned from OOF (precision of the rule >= 80%), not hand-picked.
risk: Rules tuned on Q3 may be too aggressive on other vendors; check per-vendor OOF precision.
impl_hint: rule = (d5 > q5) | (d197 > q197) | (d198 > q198) with q* = train quantiles where OOF precision >=0.8; score = score + rule*1.0 (after rank-normalising score to [0,1]).
idea: Forcing alarm=1 and a score boost for disks whose smart_5, 197 or 198 increased by a large amount inside the window (e.g., top-0.1% delta in train) while keeping ML alarms elsewhere will lift R@FAR and F1 slightly.

title: Per-vendor thresholds only with enough positives
claim: Using separate OOF-tuned thresholds for Seagate vs non-Seagate disks will improve F1 if each group has >=150 training positives, otherwise use one global threshold.
rationale: Score calibration differs across vendors/models because attribute sets differ (187/188 Seagate-only); model heterogeneity is well documented.
applicability: Only when OOF shows vendor-dependent calibration gaps.
risk: Per-group thresholds overfit quickly with few positives and hurt F1_p10.
impl_hint: t_v = argmax_t p10F1(oof[vendor==v]); shrink toward global: t = 0.5*t_v + 0.5*t_global.
idea: Using separate OOF-tuned thresholds for Seagate vs non-Seagate disks will improve F1 if each group has >=150 training positives, otherwise use one global threshold.

title: Prefer relative/change features over absolute levels under drift
claim: Emphasising deltas, rates and within-model ranks over absolute raw levels (power-on hours, LBAs, raw error totals) will reduce the Q3->Q4->Q1 generalisation gap.
rationale: StreamDFP measured distribution changes in many SMART attributes year to year and oscillating failure rates; Azure saw ~9% accuracy drops over time; relative features are less sensitive to fleet ageing and composition changes.
applicability: Always relevant because train, val and test are consecutive quarters.
risk: Some absolute levels (e.g., total reallocated sectors) remain genuinely predictive; keep them but don't rely solely on them.
impl_hint: Check OOF-to-val gap per feature group: drop groups whose importance is high but val gain is negative.
idea: Emphasising deltas, rates and within-model ranks over absolute raw levels (power-on hours, LBAs, raw error totals) will reduce the Q3->Q4->Q1 generalisation gap.

title: Borrow strength for minority models
claim: For models with <10 training failures, mapping them to the most similar failure-rich model of the same vendor (by feature distribution) or simply relying on vendor-level features will outperform per-model learning.
rationale: TLDFP selects the source model with minimal KL divergence and reweights instances (TrAdaBoost); domain-adaptive learning transfers from failure-rich to failure-poor models.
applicability: Toshiba/HGST/WDC and rare Seagate models among the ~44 models.
expected_effect: Small-medium for minority models; negligible overall if they're a small share.
risk: Wrong source mapping can hurt; keep as a feature (nearest-source id) rather than a hard switch.
impl_hint: Add 'model_family' = vendor + capacity bucket as a coarser categorical so rare models share splits.
idea: For models with <10 training failures, mapping them to the most similar failure-rich model of the same vendor (by feature distribution) or simply relying on vendor-level features will outperform per-model learning.

title: Unlabeled query features for normalization only
claim: Computing per-model normalisation statistics (medians/ranks) on train+query features, never labels, may improve alignment between Q3 training and Q4/Q1 query disks.
rationale: Domain adaptation uses unlabeled target data to align feature distributions; the benchmark forbids only labels and post-cutoff data, and query histories end at their own cutoffs.
applicability: Per-model normalisation (FE08).
risk: If the query fleet has a different model mix, stats change the meaning of features; compare with train-only stats via OOF+val.
impl_hint: stats = pd.concat([train_last, query_last]).groupby('model')[cols].median(); X = X / (stats+1).
idea: Computing per-model normalisation statistics (medians/ranks) on train+query features, never labels, may improve alignment between Q3 training and Q4/Q1 query disks.

title: Rank-average heterogeneous models
claim: Rank-averaging LightGBM (weight ~0.6), ExtraTrees (~0.25) and logistic regression on log features (~0.15) will beat the best single model on OOF weighted AUPRC and F1_p10.
rationale: No single model wins across disk models and settings (Lu 2020); the PAKDD 2020 winner ensembled LightGBM/XGBoost/CatBoost.
applicability: Once at least two reasonable models exist.
risk: Rank averaging destroys calibration; tune the alarm threshold on the blended OOF rank.
impl_hint: s = 0.6*rankdata(p_lgb)+0.25*rankdata(p_et)+0.15*rankdata(p_lr); normalise to [0,1]; tune weights on OOF.
idea: Rank-averaging LightGBM (weight ~0.6), ExtraTrees (~0.25) and logistic regression on log features (~0.15) will beat the best single model on OOF weighted AUPRC and F1_p10.

title: Seed and fold averaging for stability
claim: Averaging predictions of the 5 CV fold models (and 2-3 seeds) for the query set will reduce score variance and raise F1_p10 at negligible cost.
rationale: Bagging-style variance reduction is central to online RF/bagging for disks; with ~1100 positives, single-model variance is high.
applicability: Always when using OOF CV (also aligns query scores with OOF scale for T01).
risk: Runtime x5; still seconds for LightGBM.
impl_hint: q_pred = np.mean([m.predict_proba(Xq)[:,1] for m in fold_models], axis=0).
idea: Averaging predictions of the 5 CV fold models (and 2-3 seeds) for the query set will reduce score variance and raise F1_p10 at negligible cost.

title: Stack with a shallow meta-model only if OOF-honest
claim: A logistic-regression stacker on OOF predictions of 2-4 base models plus vendor one-hot can outperform fixed rank weights, provided stacking uses nested/OOF predictions only.
rationale: Stacking generalises fixed blending; leakage-safe OOF usage is essential (Grillmeyer).
applicability: When >=3 diverse base models exist.
risk: Easy to leak via in-sample base predictions; adds complexity for small gain.
impl_hint: meta = LogisticRegression(C=0.3).fit(np.c_[oof_lgb, oof_et, oof_lr, vendor_oh], y, sample_weight=w).
idea: A logistic-regression stacker on OOF predictions of 2-4 base models plus vendor one-hot can outperform fixed rank weights, provided stacking uses nested/OOF predictions only.

title: Evaluator static check: forbidden tokens anywhere in code
claim: Never write eval_only, holdout, val_labels, test_labels, '../', '..\', .parent, parents[, os.pardir, listdir, glob, os.walk, iterdir, scandir, rglob, getcwd, Path.cwd, chdir, subprocess, os.system, socket, urllib, requests, http.client anywhere outside '#' comments (docstrings and string literals included), or the candidate scores 0.
rationale: evaluator.py static_check scans every line (only text after '#' is stripped) with these regexes; docstrings and string literals are NOT exempt, e.g. a docstring mentioning 'holdout' or a variable named 'requests' invalidates the run.
applicability: Every generated program.
risk: Word-boundary patterns (\bglob\b, requests\b) mean names like 'requests' or 'glob' are fatal even as variables; avoid relative paths entirely.
impl_hint: Build paths only as os.path.join(args.data_dir, 'train_history.csv.gz') etc.; review generated docstrings.
idea: Never write eval_only, holdout, val_labels, test_labels, '../', '..\', .parent, parents[, os.pardir, listdir, glob, os.walk, iterdir, scandir, rglob, getcwd, Path.cwd, chdir, subprocess, os.system, socket, urllib, requests, http.client anywhere outside '#' comments (docstrings and string literals included), or the candidate scores 0.

title: Threshold chosen in-sample is the init.py weakness
claim: Replacing init.py's best_f1_threshold on training predictions with an OOF-based threshold (T01/T02) is a quick, low-risk win before any feature work.
rationale: In-sample thresholds overfit; the evaluator's bootstrap p10 explicitly punishes lucky thresholds.
applicability: Any descendant of init.py.
risk: None.
impl_hint: See T01.
idea: Replacing init.py's best_f1_threshold on training predictions with an OOF-based threshold (T01/T02) is a quick, low-risk win before any feature work.

title: Snapshot-only features cap performance
claim: Programs that use only cutoff-day values will plateau well below trend-feature programs; any evolved program lacking window deltas should get FE01/FE03 first.
rationale: Backblaze explicitly notes the need to factor time/rate into cumulative counters; time-aware features are central in Botezatu, Zhu, Xu (RNN) and StreamDFP.
applicability: Early evolution steps.
expected_effect: Large relative to other single changes.
risk: None.
impl_hint: See FE01.
idea: Programs that use only cutoff-day values will plateau well below trend-feature programs; any evolved program lacking window deltas should get FE01/FE03 first.

title: Don't expect near-perfect scores from literature
claim: Treat reported 95-98% detection rates as non-transferable; realistic targets on a strict Q3->Q4 split with 1-7 day horizon are closer to PAKDD-style F1 0.4-0.6.
rationale: Many high numbers come from row-level random splits (leakage), longer per-model histories, or unrepresentative FAR definitions; the PAKDD 2020 winner reached F1 ~0.49 on realistic data.
applicability: Setting expectations for the evolution loop (noise_delta, stopping).
risk: None.
impl_hint: Use the evaluator's f1_boot_std to set a significance margin between candidate programs.
idea: Treat reported 95-98% detection rates as non-transferable; realistic targets on a strict Q3->Q4 split with 1-7 day horizon are closer to PAKDD-style F1 0.4-0.6.

title: Avoid per-disk Python loops and heavy groupby.apply
claim: Vectorised groupby-agg and pivot-based feature construction will cut feature time from minutes to seconds versus per-serial loops, protecting time_factor.
rationale: ~31k disks x 14 days x ~30 columns per split; per-group Python callbacks dominate runtime in pandas.
applicability: All feature code.
expected_effect: Protects ROS via time_factor; enables richer features within budget.
risk: Pivot requires aligning day offsets (cutoff - date).days; handle missing days as NaN.
impl_hint: h['off']=(h.groupby('serial_number').date.transform('max')-h.date).dt.days; P=h.pivot_table(index='serial_number', columns='off', values=cols).
idea: Vectorised groupby-agg and pivot-based feature construction will cut feature time from minutes to seconds versus per-serial loops, protecting time_factor.

title: Counter resets and garbage raw values
claim: Clipping negative deltas to 0 (with a reset flag) and winsorising raw counters at the 99.9th percentile per vendor will prevent a few corrupted readings from dominating trees and rules.
rationale: Production SMART data has inaccurate or missing samples (RODMAN); schema/firmware changes alter values between quarters (Backblaze docs).
applicability: All raw counter features.
risk: Genuine huge jumps are the strongest signals; winsorise at a very high quantile only.
impl_hint: delta = (last-first); reset = delta < 0; delta = delta.clip(lower=0); x = x.clip(upper=x.quantile(0.999)).
idea: Clipping negative deltas to 0 (with a reset flag) and winsorising raw counters at the 99.9th percentile per vendor will prevent a few corrupted readings from dominating trees and rules.
